rationale: The book's entry glosses Faith as 'Faithfulness — obedience held steady by hope in the promise,' printed with Hab 2:4 and Jas 2:17. On those cited texts the book's identification is the stronger fit: the Hebrew of Habakkuk 2:4 is emunah, which lexically means steadfastness/faithfulness (the book corroborates this with the word's first occurrence, Moses' hands 'steady'—emunah—in Exodus 17:12), and James 2:17 states outright that faith without works is dead. The strongest counter — the mainstream reading that faith is inner trusting reliance of which obedience is merely the fruit — must route Hab 2:4 through Paul's Greek reappropriation against the Hebrew, and must read James's 'dead, being alone' as describing absent evidence rather than absent substance, a softer fit to James's own language ('faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect,' Jas 2:22). The book also independently grounds its secondary elaboration ('held steady by hope') in Heb 11:1 with Rom 8:24-25, and its trust-obedience unity in texts whose Greek genuinely supports it: John 3:36 opposes believing to apeithein (disobeying), and Heb 3:18-19 equates unbelief with disobedience. Notably, the book does not deny trust — it defines faith as 'the trust that obeys' — so it subsumes the counter's referent while explaining the cited texts more exactly. The Pauline faith/works antithesis (Rom 4:4-5; Eph 2:8-9) remains the counter's best material, but those texts are not printed with the entry, the book has a coherent available move (Gen 15:6 belief and Jas 2:21 obedience treated as one act; 'works' as wage-earning merit), and mainstream scholarship (the pistis-as-allegiance/faithfulness reading, which Response A itself lists as a common view) holds the same position without contradiction. No supplied text is inexplicable on the book's core; the book carries its cited texts better than the counter carries them.
book_core_identification: Biblical 'faith' (emunah/pistis) denotes faithfulness: steadfast obedience to God's commandments held constant in hope of the unseen promise — an enacted covenant loyalty, not a mental state of assent or bare inner trust of which works are only a downstream effect.
book_secondary_elaborations: The motive-office distinction: faith keeps the commandments specifically 'in hope of the promise,' distinguishing it from love (the keeping itself), knowing (covenant union), and belief (keeping because it is true).
Hebrews 11:1 read as faith being the visible 'evidence' member of the seen/unseen pair — conduct standing in where sight is denied.
The lexical anchor in Exodus 17:12 (emunah = steady hands) as the word's first-occurrence picture.
'Works' defined as commandment-shaped deeds via Exodus 18:20, Psalm 111:7, and Revelation 2:26.
The claim that believing and obeying are one act (John 3:36 apeithōn; Heb 3:18; Rom 10:16; Gen 15:6 with Jas 2:21).
strongest_counter_interpretation: Faith is fundamentally inward trusting reliance on God and his promise — the receptive instrument of justification — which necessarily produces obedience as its fruit but is not itself constituted by obedience. On this reading Hab 2:4 as Paul deploys it (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11) means the righteous live by believing trust; Jas 2:14-26 teaches that works are the evidence certifying living faith, not its substance; and the sharp Pauline antitheses (Rom 4:4-5, 'to him that worketh not, but believeth'; Eph 2:8-9, 'through faith... not of works') show faith cannot be identified with works of obedience.
counter_core_identification: Faith = confident personal trust in God/Christ and his promises, prior to and productive of obedience, but categorically distinct from the works it produces.
material_core_denial: The counter denies the book's identity claim: obedience is the fruit and evidence of faith, not the thing faith is; therefore 'faith' cannot be defined as faithfulness/obedience-held-in-hope without collapsing the Pauline distinction between faith and works.
counter_case: Rom 4:4-5 explicitly contrasts the one 'that worketh not, but believeth' whose faith is counted for righteousness — hard to square with faith defined as obedient works.
Eph 2:8-9: saved 'through faith... not of works, lest any man should boast' — if faith is constituted by works, the sentence approaches self-contradiction.
Gen 15:6: Abraham's faith is counted righteous at the moment of believing a promise, decades before the offering of Isaac.
Paul's citation of Hab 2:4 (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11) functions in an argument about believing, suggesting he read pistis there as trust.
Mark 11:22-24 and Heb 11:1 read naturally as inner assurance and confident expectation in prayer, not as enacted steadiness.
James 2 can be read as faith being evidenced (shown, Jas 2:18) by works rather than constituted by them.
book_explanatory_advantages: Hab 2:4's Hebrew emunah lexically means faithfulness/steadfastness, exactly matching the book's gloss; the counter must override the Hebrew with Paul's Greek appropriation.
The first occurrence of emunah (Exod 17:12, Moses' hands 'steady... until the going down of the sun') is a picture of held-steady action, corroborating faithfulness over inner conviction.
Jas 2:17 (the entry's other printed text) states the book's thesis nearly verbatim; Jas 2:19 (demons' perfect assent saves none) and 2:22 support constitution, not mere evidence.
John 3:36's Greek opposes 'believeth' to apeithōn ('obeyeth not'), and Heb 3:18-19 equates unbelief with disobedience — one act named from two sides, as the book claims.

Hebrews 11 is in fact a catalog of visible obediences ('By faith Abraham... obeyed,' 11:8; Noah 'prepared an ark,' 11:7), matching 'obedience held steady by hope' with the hope-objects the book names (11:10, 16).
The 'held steady by hope' clause is independently grounded: Rom 8:24-25 ties unseen hope to patient endurance, and 2 Cor 5:7 sets conduct where sight is denied.
The book subsumes rather than excludes trust ('the trust that obeys'), so it explains the trust-texts while the pure-trust counter cannot as naturally explain the obedience-texts.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Rom 4:4-5 and Eph 2:8-9 read most naturally on a faith/works distinction; the book's chapter never directly addresses either text.
Gen 15:6's timing (righteousness credited upon believing a promise) fits receptive trust straightforwardly.
Prayer-faith texts (Mark 11:22-24; Matt 17:20) are more naturally 'confidence God will act' than 'steadfast obedience.'
It matches the dominant confessional and lexical tradition for NT pistis in soteriological contexts.
decisive_sources: Habakkuk 2:4 (MT emunah = faithfulness/steadfastness — the entry's own printed text)
James 2:17 with 2:19-22 (faith without works dead; wrought with works, made perfect by works)
Exodus 17:12 (first occurrence of emunah: hands held steady)
Hebrews 11:1 with 11:7-10 and Romans 8:24-25 (faith as the seen conduct answering unseen hope)
John 3:36 (Greek apeithōn: believing opposed to disobeying) and Hebrews 3:18-19 (unbelief = disobedience)
unresolved_objections: The book does not directly engage Rom 4:4-5 or Eph 2:8-9, the Pauline texts most resistant to identifying faith with obedient works; its implicit answer (works = wage-earning merit / works of the law, with Gen 15:6 and Jas 2:21 treated as one act) is available but not argued in the supplied material.

The exclusivity of the gloss: many NT prayer and miracle contexts (Mark 11:22-24) use pistis for confident expectation, which 'faithfulness' captures less naturally; the book's 'trust that obeys' concedes trust but the entry headword 'Faithfulness' alone could over-narrow.
The pistis Christou debate is untouched: if key Pauline instances mean Christ's own faithfulness, some of the book's supporting texts describe Christ's fidelity rather than the believer's.
